newsitem.title: USA: U.S. gave citizenship to people with crime records.
newsitem.headline: U.S. gave citizenship to people with crime records.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department has told Congress it is reviewing cases where it may have granted citizenship to people with criminal records because it failed to do required background checks, two lawmakers said Monday.

Assistant Attorney General Stephen Colgate told two House subcommittees that of the more than 1 million individuals naturalised from August 1995 to September 1996, about 180,000 applicants' criminal records were not reviewed.

Of those applicants that did undergo background checks, 71,557 had criminal records ranging from minor offences to serious crimes such as drug trafficking and rape, but were granted citizenship anyway, Colgate told the subcommitees.

A statement late Monday outlining Colgate's testimony was released by Chairman Lamar Smith of the House Immigration Subcommittee and Chairman Dennis Hastert of the Subcommittee on National Security, International Affairs and Criminal Justice. Smith is a Texas Republican while Hastert is a Republican from Illinois.

Attorney General Janet Reno in December rejected a request by five House Republicans for an independent investigation into the Immigration and Naturalisation Service's Citizenship USA programme to naturalise a record 1.3 million new citizens.
Republicans charge the Clinton administration rushed the naturalisation programme for political gain, believing new citizens would vote Democratic in the 1996 presidential election.

"Assistant Attorney General Colgate's disclosure confirms our worst fears: that in its unprecedented push to rush through a million new citizens, potential voters all, the INS may have allowed dangerous criminals onto our streets, all the while denying it was doing exactly that," Hastert said in a statement.
He said the Justice Department finally appeared to be giving the matter the attention it deserved and was holding the responsible parties accountable.
The two subcommittees will hold a joint hearing on the issue next month.
